title: Special circumstances: sensitivities, co-located aged care and kitchenette products
audience: Cleaners, supervisors and unit managers in SA healthcare facilities, including those with aged care beds on the same site
learningOutcomes: Identify when the standard schedule might have to be adjusted
Name who must agree a change to the schedule or product
Select products that meet the kitchenette requirement in a clinical setting

instruction.heading: Adjusting for a patient's condition
instruction.body: The standard allows the schedule to deviate where a patient's medical condition calls for it. One example is a patient with multiple chemical sensitivities, who may react to routine cleaning products. The facility can then plan a different product or method for that area. Any such change is agreed with clinical management and the infection prevention service. The SA policy guideline on idiopathic environmental intolerance and multiple chemical sensitivity (2016) covers the wider context; its text is not reproduced here.

instruction.heading: Aged care beside acute beds
instruction.body: Some facilities, particularly in rural areas, have aged care residents in the same building as acute patients. In those settings the cadence of cleaning and spot cleaning in shared areas might need to rise to match the risk of body fluid contamination. Raise the gap with clinical management and the infection prevention team, and record the agreed change.

instruction.heading: Kitchenettes in clinical areas
instruction.body: Where food is handled in a clinical or ward setting, such as a kitchenette, every detergent and sanitiser used there needs food-grade status and no perfume. This rule is separate from the disinfectants used on patient surfaces. A fragranced general spray is not acceptable in a kitchenette, whatever it is used for elsewhere in the building.

procedure: Check the patient's care notes or the ward record for any sensitivity flag.
If a sensitivity is recorded, ask the unit manager which product and method to use.
In a kitchenette, check that each product is food grade and free of perfume before use.
In a site with aged care beds, check the schedule for shared common areas and raise any gap.
Record any change and the person who approved it.

workedExamples.situation: A ward kitchenette is cleaned with a fragranced general spray. A patient on the ward has a documented sensitivity to fragrance.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop using the fragranced product in that area and ask the unit manager for a fragrance-free option. The kitchenette rule means the fragranced spray is not acceptable there in any case, so the product should be replaced whether or not the sensitivity existed.

equipmentAndPpe: Care note or ward record for sensitivity flags

commonErrors.error: Changing a product because a staff member has a hunch about a patient
commonErrors.prevention: Changes are agreed with the unit manager and the infection prevention team.

commonErrors.error: Using a general cleaner in a kitchenette
commonErrors.prevention: Check the label for food grade status and the absence of perfume.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Patient sensitivity information is private health information. Share it only with staff who need it for the task.
The 2016 policy guideline is named only.

qualityStandard: The learner names one circumstance that can change the schedule
The learner states the kitchenette product rule
documentationEvidence: Record of any agreed product or method change, with the approver and date
summary: A documented patient sensitivity can change the product or method, once agreed
Kitchenette products need food-grade status and no perfume
Aged care beside acute beds may need more frequent common-area cleaning

knowledgeChecks.question: A patient has a documented chemical sensitivity. Who agrees a change to the cleaning product?
options: The cleaner alone, on the day, with no one else
Clinical management, with the infection prevention service
The patient's family only and the visitors who come on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: What must detergent and sanitiser in a clinical kitchenette be?
options: Food grade and free of perfume

knowledgeChecks.question: When may common-area cleaning in co-located aged care need to increase?
options: Only at weekends, when visitors are few and the staff are light
When the risk of body fluid contamination makes it necessary
Only when a visitor reports a spill in the lounge area
